content: MT-TE, also known as mitochondrially encoded tRNA glutamic acid, is a transfer RNA (tRNA) molecule encoded by the mitochondrial MT-TE gene in humans. This tRNA is composed of 69 nucleotides and is located at position 14674-14742 on the human mitochondrial genome. Its primary function is to transfer the amino acid glutamic acid to a growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during protein synthesis. Structure The MT-TE gene is situated on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 68 base pairs. The tRNA molecule encoded by this gene has a distinctive folded structure, characterized by three hairpin loops, resembling a three-leafed clover. Function The MT-TE gene encodes a specific tRNA known as tRNA^Glu. This tRNA is responsible for binding to glutamic acid (Glu) and incorporating it into the appropriate positions of the growing peptide chain during protein synthesis. The tRNA^Glu molecule is localized within the mitochondria and plays a critical role in assembling proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation. Clinical Significance Mutations in the MT-TE gene can lead to mitochondrial deficiencies and associated disorders. Maternally Inherited Diabetes and Deafness (MIDD) A mutation in the MT-TE gene has been identified in individuals with maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD). This condition is characterized by diabetes and, in some cases, hearing loss, particularly affecting high-frequency sounds. Additional symptoms may include muscle weakness (myopathy) and complications involving the eyes, heart, or kidneys. The mutation likely disrupts mitochondrial function, impairing insulin release. In affected individuals, diabetes arises when beta cells fail to produce sufficient insulin to regulate blood sugar levels. The exact mechanism by which these mutations cause hearing loss or other features of MIDD remains unclear. The mutation associated with this condition involves the substitution of thymine with cytosine at position 14709 (T14709C). A family with the 14709T>C mutation exhibited phenotypes including congenital myopathy, mental retardation, cerebellar ataxia, and diabetes mellitus. Another patient with the same mutation presented with type 1 diabetes mellitus, severe myopathy, and high-frequency hearing loss, suggesting maternal inheritance. Infantile Transient Mitochondrial Myopathy Infantile transient mitochondrial myopathy, also known as benign COX deficiency myopathy, is a rare condition occurring in infancy. It is characterized by severe muscle weakness, hypotonia (poor muscle tone), and lactic acidosis (accumulation of lactic acid in the body). Affected infants often require respiratory support and have feeding difficulties. However, symptoms typically improve after several months, and most affected individuals are asymptomatic by the age of 2 or 3. Mutations associated with this condition alter single nucleotides in mitochondrial DNA, impairing oxidative phosphorylation. Consequently, muscle cells fail to produce sufficient energy, leading to the observed muscle problems. The reasons why only muscles are affected and how recovery occurs remain unknown. Specific mutations, such as 14674T>G and 14674T>C, have been identified in patients with this myopathy. Complex IV Deficiency MT-TE mutations have also been linked to complex IV deficiency of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, also known as cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. This rare genetic condition can affect multiple organ systems, including skeletal muscles, the heart, the brain, and the liver. Common clinical manifestations include myopathy, hypotonia, encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A substitution mutation, 14680C>A, has been identified in a patient with this deficiency.
